'''Preservation, Fermentation and Spice Reference'''
Compiled for the Van Kush Family Research Institute / Botanica Coffee Co. Working
reference — pickling, fermenting, spice blends, and the growing plan that feeds them.

== I. Pickling Spice — Full Ingredient Range ==

=== Foundation ===
The four that appear in nearly every standard blend:

   Mustard seed — yellow (Sinapis alba) is mild and acts as a thickener; brown (B. juncea)
   is the Dijon workhorse; black (B. nigra) is sharpest and is the Indian and South Asian
   standard, bloomed in hot oil until it pops. These are not interchangeable — a blend using
   all three has more layered heat than yellow alone. Black and brown are cheap at any
   Indian grocery.

   Black peppercorns — steady classic heat

   Coriander seed — bright, faintly citrus

   Bay leaf — grounding and savory; crumble for blends

=== Sweet and warm accents ===
   Allspice berries — reads as clove, cinnamon and nutmeg together

   Cloves — aggressive; use sparingly

   Cinnamon stick — broken into pieces

   Dried ginger — cracked, sharp and zesty

=== Savory and spicy accents ===
   Dill seed — essential to classic dill pickles, far stronger than fresh dill weed

   Red pepper flakes

   Celery seed — concentrated savory vegetable depth; the deli-pickle note
=== Extended range — seeds and warm spices ===
Fenugreek (bitter-savory, central to Indian pickles) · nigella / kalonji · caraway · fennel · star
anise · juniper berries (excellent with cabbage and game) · grains of paradise · cardamom
pods · mace

=== Extended range — fresh and leaf ===
Grape, oak and horseradish leaves (tannin sources — see firming agents below) · fresh bay ·
tarragon · thyme · summer savory · lovage · sorrel · shiso

=== Extended range — alliums and heat ===
Garlic · shallot · whole dried chiles · Sichuan peppercorn · long pepper · cubeb

=== Regional templates ===
    Indian — black mustard, fenugreek, nigella, asafoetida, turmeric

    Japanese (tsukemono) — kombu, shiso, yuzu peel

    Middle Eastern (torshi) — mint, dill, turmeric, Aleppo pepper

== II. Firming Agents — and the Lime Question ==
Do not use pickling lime for flavor work. Calcium hydroxide is not a spice and contributes
nothing to taste. Its only function is firming pectin in produce destined for long storage, and
it works by pre-soaking raw vegetables 12–24 hours before brining, followed by three rinses
in fresh water. For anything seasoned over a day or two there is no mechanism by which it
helps.

There is also a real hazard: residual lime raises pH, and in a sealed low-acid jar that is the
condition C. botulinum favors. USDA removed it from recommended methods for this
reason.

=== Use instead: ===

    Calcium chloride (Pickle Crisp) — modern replacement. Added directly to the jar. No
    soaking, no rinsing, no pH shift.

    Tannin-bearing leaves — grape, oak, horseradish, or black tea. These are the
    traditional answer; tannins inhibit the enzyme that softens pickles. Horseradish is useful
    here twice over, since the plant supplies both the root for grating and the leaf for the jar.
III. Ferments

=== Starting points ===
   Sauerkraut — cabbage, 2% salt by weight, nothing else. The one to learn the process
   on.

   Kimchi — napa cabbage, gochugaru, garlic, ginger, fish sauce

   Curtido — Salvadoran: cabbage, carrot, onion, oregano. Fast and mild.

   Giardiniera — cauliflower, carrot, celery, hot pepper; brined then packed in oil. Chicago-
   Italian households make this constantly and often store it in whatever container is at
   hand. (The “Piggly” in the water bottle is almost certainly this. The alternative candidate
   is Southern chow-chow, but the vegetable list matches giardiniera.)

   Lacto dill pickles — cucumbers in 3.5% brine with a tannin leaf

=== Fermented hot sauce — method ===
# Stem the chiles; seeds optional. Pack into a jar with garlic and any aromatics.

# Cover with 3–5% brine by weight — 30–50 g salt per liter of water. Use 5% in Texas
   summer heat, 3% when cool.

# Weight everything below the liquid line.

# Room temperature, 7–21 days. It will bubble and turn cloudy, then settle. Longer
   ferment yields more sour and more complex.

# Blend with some of the brine. Add vinegar to taste for shelf stability. Strain for a smooth
   sauce.

Variations: mango or pineapple in the ferment (fruit sugars feed it) · carrot for body and
sweetness · roasted garlic stirred in after fermentation · smoked chiles for chipotle
character.

Note: jalapeño jelly is unrelated — a sweet pectin preserve of peppers, sugar, vinegar and
pectin, cooked and set. Served over cream cheese. Classic Texas market product, but not a
ferment.

=== Fermented garlic honey ===
Peel cloves, cover with raw honey, flip the jar daily so the cloves stay coated.

The mechanism: honey is normally too low in moisture to support microbial life, but garlic is
roughly 60% water. The garlic releases moisture, diluting the honey enough that wild yeasts
and lactobacilli already present on the cloves become active. It bubbles for several weeks.
Ready in about a month, keeps indefinitely. The garlic loses its raw bite and turns syrupy
and mellow.

Safety: honey can carry C. botulinum spores and this is a low-acid anaerobic environment.
Add a tablespoon of vinegar to bring pH below 4.6. Cheap insurance.

Tepache
Pineapple rind and core — the parts normally discarded — plus water and piloncillo or brown
sugar. Cinnamon and clove optional. Covered, room temperature, 2–4 days, then strain and
chill. Lightly fizzy, tart-sweet, minimal alcohol.

The entire appeal is that it is made from waste, which makes it a natural fit alongside
produce-rescue sourcing.

Beyond vegetables
Kefir (milk or water — the water version takes fruit and herbs well) · kombucha · jun (honey-
based, accepts botanicals readily) · miso and koji (long project, deep payoff) · sourdough ·
preserved lemons (salt only)

Mead follows directly from garlic honey: honey, water, yeast. A 1-gallon carboy is most of
the equipment. Metheglin — mead with herbs and spices — is where botanical work
naturally goes.

== IV. Vinegar Pickles — Fast Turnaround ==
Red onion · jalapeño · carrot · beet · green bean (dilly beans) · okra · radish · daikon ·
cauliflower · eggplant · mushroom · watermelon rind · eggs

Gari (sushi ginger)
Young ginger, salt, rice vinegar, sugar. Slice paper-thin, salt briefly, blanch, pack in the
sweetened vinegar. A quick pickle rather than a ferment — ready in a day or two, keeps for
months refrigerated.

On the color: real gari turns pale pink on its own because young ginger contains
anthocyanins that react with acid. Mature ginger will not, which is why commercial versions
use dye or a slice of beet. Beige is not a failure.

Why young ginger: thin skin, tender, no fibrous strings. Mature grocery ginger makes a
harsh, stringy pickle. Growing ginger in a container and harvesting early is the only reliable
way to get young ginger outside its brief market season.

The same technique works on carrot, daikon and lotus root.

== V. Chicken — Pickle Flavoring ==
Method: pickle brine into a ziplock bag with the chicken, refrigerate, discard the bag
afterward. No firming agent — there is nothing to firm.

   Timing: 2–4 hours for pieces, up to overnight for thighs. Past roughly 12 hours the acid
   leaves the surface chalky.

   Pat dry before cooking. Wet from brine means it steams instead of browning.

   Do not reuse brine that has contacted raw chicken. Keep a separate pouring jar.

   Flavor drivers: dill seed, mustard seed, coriander, black pepper, garlic, celery seed, and
   the vinegar itself. Bay and allspice sit in the background.

   For a dry rub version: grind the same spices and add citric acid or powdered vinegar
   for the sour note.

== VI. Horseradish and Mustard — Product Range ==
Horseradish, wasabi, mustard, radish and arugula all produce isothiocyanates from
glucosinolates when their cells rupture. Same compound family, differing intensity — which
is why they substitute for one another in principle, and why the heat registers in the sinuses
rather than on the tongue the way capsaicin does.

Horseradish-based
   Prepared horseradish — grated root, vinegar, salt. The control is timing: vinegar added
   immediately keeps it mild; waiting 2–3 minutes makes it fierce.

   Cocktail sauce — ketchup, horseradish, lemon, Worcestershire

   Horseradish cream — sour cream or crème fraîche base, for beef

   Chrain — Ashkenazi, with beet; sweet-sharp and deep magenta

   Bloody Mary mix

   Compound butter — freezes well
Mustard-based
   Whole grain — soak seeds in vinegar with beer or wine, blend partially. Best value and
   easiest.

   Dijon-style — brown seeds, white wine

   Honey mustard · beer mustard

   Hot Chinese mustard — mustard powder and cold water; the enzyme reaction only
   occurs cold

   Mostarda — Italian, fruit candied in mustard syrup

   Mustard oil pickles — Indian style

Both prepared horseradish and whole grain mustard are shelf-stable, high-margin, and
made from inputs that can be grown or bought cheaply in bulk.

On wasabi
Real wasabi (Wasabia japonica / Eutrema japonicum) is in the same family as horseradish
and mustard. Almost nothing sold as wasabi is wasabi — the tube product and most
restaurant paste is horseradish, mustard powder and green dye.

It is among the most expensive crops in the world (roughly $100+/lb) because cultivation is
genuinely difficult: cold running water, deep shade, 46–70°F, high humidity, and 18 months
to two years to harvest. Even commercial growers lose crops routinely.

Fresh-grated, it is aromatic and nearly sweet, with heat that hits the nose and fades in about
fifteen minutes — the compounds begin degrading within minutes of grating, which is why it
is grated tableside on a sharkskin grater.

Not viable in North Texas outdoors. Horseradish is the practical substitute, and is what is
in the tube regardless.

VII. Growing Plan

Start from the produce section — free plant stock
From roots and bases: ginger and turmeric (pieces with visible growth buds, planted
shallow in a wide pot) · garlic · potato and sweet potato · lemongrass (stalks root in water in
about two weeks) · green onion, leek, celery, bok choy, cabbage, romaine (regrow from the
cut base in shallow water, then transplant) · horseradish
From seed inside the produce: hot peppers especially · tomatoes (ferment the seeds a few
days, rinse, dry) · winter squash, pumpkin, melon · dry beans, lentils and chickpeas from the
dry goods aisle

Herb cuttings — root in water: basil, mint, rosemary, thyme, oregano, cilantro. Mint and
basil root in under two weeks. A $2 clamshell becomes a Mediterranean bed.

Won’t work: hybrid apples and citrus will not come true from seed. Some ginger and
potatoes carry sprout inhibitor — organic avoids this.

Note: SNAP purchases both produce and seed packets. For heterosis work, produce-
section seed is open-pollinated in some cases and hybrid in others — worth recording
which, since F2 segregation from a hybrid tomato is data rather than failure.

Fall planting window — October to November, North Texas

  Crop        Notes

              Break head into cloves, skin on, pointy end up, 2” deep, 4–6” apart. Needs cold
              exposure to split into a head — spring planting yields one fat single bulb instead.
  Garlic      Softneck types suit Texas: ‘Texas Early White’, ‘Inchelium Red’, ‘Lorz Italian’.
              Mulch, don’t overwater, stop watering weeks before harvest. Harvest when the
              lower third of leaves brown; cure in shade with airflow.

              Same method but shallower — tip at or just below the surface, 6” apart. Each
              clove multiplies into a cluster of 5–10. No cold requirement, higher multiplication
  Shallots
              rate, more forgiving than garlic. Grocery shallots work; rarely sprout-treated.
              Save the best cluster to replant and you never buy them again.

              Direct seed late August–October. 50–70 days. Needs loose, deep soil for the
  Daikon      taproot. Doubles as a cover crop — the root breaks compaction and decomposes
              in place. Feeds takuan, kimchi and quick pickles off one crop.

              Bolts hard in Texas summer — plant fall or very early spring, never August. Fall
  Dill        planting in Zone 8 often overwinters for a long spring harvest. Self-seeds
              aggressively; plant once and get volunteers for years.

Dill varieties — they are genuinely different plants
    Mammoth / Mammoth Long Island — bred for seed heads. Tall (4–5 ft), bolts fast,
    large umbels. The pickling dill.

    Bouquet — all-purpose. Good foliage and good heads, more compact. Best single
    choice for pickling plus spice blending.
    Dukat — bred for leaf. Slow to bolt, sweeter foliage, longer productive window. For fresh
    dill weed.

Horseradish
Easy to the point of being a problem — famously invasive, since any root fragment left
behind regrows.

Grow it in a container. Five-gallon bucket or half barrel, 18–24” deep. Solves the spreading
entirely and makes harvest a matter of dumping the pot.

Hardy to Zone 3 and tolerant of heat, but prefers cool. The west-facing bed is wrong — full
Texas afternoon sun will stress it. Partial shade, balcony or east side.

Plant a root cutting (not seed) in early spring; harvest in fall after frost, when flavor
sharpens with cold. One cutting yields a great deal; save pieces to replant. A grocery root
will often start if untreated — costs nothing to try.

West-facing bed — what belongs there
Brutal afternoon sun from about 2 p.m. onward suits Mediterranean herbs, which produce
more essential oil under that stress: rosemary, thyme, oregano, sage, lavender, Greek
oregano. Also bay laurel, za’atar, and an established fig.

On raspberries: among the few berries that genuinely struggle in DFW — they want chill
and dislike sustained heat above 90°F, and a west bed is the hardest possible placement.
Either use the heat-tolerant cultivars (‘Dorman Red’, ‘Bababerry’) or switch to blackberries
— ‘Brazos’, ‘Rosborough’, ‘Kiowa’ were bred by Texas A&M for this climate and fruit heavily
with little fuss.

Timing: prep soil now — compost worked in, heavy mulch. Herb transplants late
September–October. Brambles bare-root December–February.

VIII. Practical Notes
    A kitchen scale is the one non-negotiable tool. Salt percentage by weight is the entire
    game in fermentation.

    Toasting whole spices before they meet liquid extracts more in an hour than a longer
    cold soak will.

    Fermentation is the natural partner to dehydrating on produce-rescue sourcing: what
    can’t be dried gets fermented. It is the traditional answer to too much cheap produce
   arriving at once.

   Coffee is itself a fermented product — the wet process is a controlled ferment. The
   microbiology overlaps with the roasting side more than is generally appreciated.

   Before selling anything: Texas cottage food law covers pickles and some ferments but
   carries specific pH and labeling requirements. Read them before Botanica sells any of it.

Prepared July 2026. Growing dates are calibrated to USDA Zone 8, North Texas.
